Article Title: In 2020, Minnesota funded a $1.918 million Shell Rock River habitat program; by 2025, it had protected or restored 588 acres
Article Text:
Shell Rock River Watershed District (Image Credit: www.shellrock.org)

A habitat program takes shape

Three properties protected

Wetlands and prairie restored

More acres than planned

A longer-term conservation effort

In 2020, Minnesota approved $1.918 million for the Shell Rock River Watershed Habitat Restoration Program - Phase IX. According to a 2025 final report from the Lessard-Sams Outdoor Heritage Council, the program ultimately protected, restored or enhanced 588 acres of habitat in the Shell Rock River watershed, exceeding its original goal of 483 acres.The funding was provided under Minnesota Laws 2020, with the appropriation directed to the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources for an agreement with the Shell Rock River Watershed District. The funding was intended to support land acquisition as well as the restoration and enhancement of aquatic habitat within the watershed. The program focused on several types of conservation work, including acquiring properties, restoring wetlands and improving aquatic habitat. The projects were selected using conservation planning and monitoring intended to identify areas where habitat improvements could provide significant benefits.The Shell Rock River Watershed is a shallow-lake system that supports fish, waterfowl and other wildlife. According to the final report, restoration projects were targeted at addressing habitat degradation and improving conditions for native fish, waterfowl and wildlife.One part of Phase IX involved acquiring three properties: the Glenville Property, the Bancroft Property, and the Church Lake Property. The District closed on the Glenville Property in March 2021 and the Bancroft Property in September 2021. For the Church Lake Property, the District transferred the deed to the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources in December 2024 after acquiring and restoring the parcel.The final report says these acquisitions contributed to the program's permanent protection of 218 acres. Another 370 acres of habitat and wetlands were enhanced or restored through the program. Together, those accomplishments contributed to the reported total of 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored.The program included several restoration projects beyond property acquisition. The Bancroft Wetland Restoration was initiated in 2020, with construction beginning in June 2024 and largely completed by the fall of that year. Additional seeding work was completed in spring 2025. Another project focused on Panicum Prairie, where habitat enhancement work was carried out across 300 acres. The project involved native prairie vegetation and was substantially completed in February 2025, with final work completed in May.The program also supported the Fountain Lake In-Lake Habitat Project. Work included additional rock reefs and rock boulder clusters intended to improve fish habitat. The report notes that Phase IX funds were used to expand the scope of this work after the District determined additional funds were available. These projects addressed different parts of the watershed's ecosystem, from wetlands and prairie habitat to aquatic areas. The broader aim was to improve habitat conditions while protecting areas that could provide long-term benefits for wildlife.The program's original accomplishment plan called for 483 acres. By the end of the project, the final total had reached 588 acres, 105 acres more than initially planned. The report attributes the increase to the addition of the In-Lake Habitat Project and the Church Lake Property to Phase IX.According to the report, all grant funds were spent. The final grant expenditure remained $1.918 million, while the program's final total including leverage was $1.9479 million.The work is intended to continue beyond the end of the grant. The Shell Rock River Watershed District relies on multiple funding sources, including a local option sales tax, local levy and public funding, to maintain conservation projects. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources will also maintain the Church Lake Property, which it owns.The program's results illustrate how a single state-funded conservation effort can combine land protection, wetland restoration, prairie enhancement and aquatic habitat improvements. Rather than focusing on one habitat type, Phase IX combined several projects across the Shell Rock River watershed. By 2025, the program had moved beyond its original target, with the final report recording 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored. The completed work represents a combination of permanent land protection and habitat improvements designed to support Minnesota's fish, waterfowl and wildlife over the long term.
Article Summary: In 2020, Minnesota approved $1.918 million for the Shell Rock River Watershed Habitat Restoration Program - Phase IX. By 2025, the program had moved beyond its original target, with the final report recording 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored.

Article Title: Upset Paramount may leave California; company says it has duty towards shareholders, and that ultimately, you go to the place where you ...
Article Text:
Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. merger under fire

Jobs and economy

Paramount Skydance reported mixed earnings results

Paramount Skydance’s chief legal officer Makan Delrahim has suggested that the company could leave California as it faces mounting antitrust scrutiny from the state government. According to a report by The Hill, speaking at Politico’s The The California Agenda: Sacramento Summit, Delrahim said CEO David Ellison remains committed to California but emphasized there is a point where the company has a fiduciary duty to shareholders. “You have to take a look at the business environment and look to see what’s best for not only the community and the business. And ultimately, you know, go to the place where you’re wanted,” he said.Paramount, based in Los Angeles, agreed last month to pause its multibillion-dollar acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery after litigation was filed by California’s attorney general and 11 other states. The lawsuit argues the deal would give Paramount excessive power in news, entertainment, and sports media, harming competition. A trial is scheduled for next spring.The merger has drawn criticism from Democrats and media watchdogs, who worry that Warner Bros.Discovery’s CNN could fall under the influence of Ellison, an ally of President Trump and son of Oracle founder Larry Ellison. Ellison defended the deal in a New York Times op-ed, writing: “I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views.”Delrahim argued the lawsuit is harming employment, saying: “This merger is actually going to be good — not only for California — it’ll be good for America.” Paramount maintains that its duty to shareholders may ultimately force it to relocate if California continues to oppose the merger.Recently, Paramount Skydance reported mixed second-quarter results, with revenue rising 1% year-over-year to $6.91 billion, beating estimates, while profit fell short at $41 million. Streaming revenue grew 9% to nearly $2.5 billion, driven by subscriber gains from Paramount+ content including UFC Freedom 250 and the FIFA World Cup. Studio revenue reached $1.3 billion, though theatrical performance lagged compared to last year’s Mission: Impossible — The Final Reckoning.
Article Summary: Paramount Skydance’s chief legal officer Makan Delrahim has suggested that the company could leave California as it faces mounting antitrust scrutiny. Delrahim said CEO David Ellison remains committed to California but emphasized there is a point where the company has a fiduciary duty to shareholders.

Article Title: Phoebe Gates’ shopping app Phia responds to 'cookie stuffing' allegations, says have started issuing ...
Article Text:
Phoebe Gates' Phia responds to cookie stuffing allegations

What Phia spokesperson said

What is cookie stuffing that Phoebe Gates’ Phia is accused of

Phia, the AI-powered shopping startup founded by Bill Gates daughter Phoebe Gates and her Stanford roommate Sophia Kianni said that it is reviewing every transaction carefully and will reverse sales that were incorrectly attributed to it, says a report by People. The development comes days after a Bloomberg report said that the two founders were aware of ‘cookie stuffing’ – a practice where affiliate tracking cookies are placed on a user's browser without their knowledge, allowing a company to claim commission on purchases even when it did not influence the sale. The report cites internal Slack messages, people familiar with the matter and historical source code saying that both Gates and Kianni were aware of automatic cookie-setting features months earlier.The People report quotes a Phia spokesperson who told the publication:“Any features causing misattributions were immediately removed over a month ago on July 7. We are reviewing every transaction, we are fully committed to and have already begun issuing all transaction reversals to brand partners as a result of any misattribution, and we are hiring a head of compliance to make sure something like this never happens again.”“We are now continuing to connect our users with items and offers from thousands of brand partners,” the spokesperson continued, further adding “We will learn from this and want to ensure our users have the best possible shopping experience, with features like our new digital closet and more to come.”The statement did not address Bloomberg’s latest accusationsPhia operates as a browser extension designed to help shoppers automatically find discount codes and compare prices at online checkout counters. In exchange, partner retailers pay the platform an affiliate commission when its software helps convert a sale.However, internal chats accessed by the publication reveal that Phia implemented automated features that injected its tracking cookies into a shopper’s checkout session without requiring any user interaction, such as clicking a deal link or applying a coupon code, the Bloomberg report said. By dropping tracking identifiers automatically, Phia claimed credit and commissions for transactions it did not drive, a practice widely known as cookie stuffing and that is strictly prohibited by commercial network contracts and partner agreements.
Article Summary: Phia, the AI-powered shopping startup founded by Bill Gates daughter Phoebe Gates and her Stanford roommate Sophia Kianni said that it is reviewing every transaction carefully and will reverse sales that were incorrectly attributed to it. The development comes days after a Bloomberg report said that the two founders were aware of ‘cookie stuffing’ – a practice where affiliate tracking cookies are placed on a user's browser without their knowledge.

Article Title: China takes aim at Elon Musk’s ‘Jesus-level’ brain-chip dream with first BCI surgery policy
Article Text:
Repesentative image

A first-of-its-kind insurance policy

How the technology works

The 'Jesus-level technology'

Clinical trials in China and safety concerns

Government push

Elon Musk has spent years pursuing what he has called "Jesus-level" technology through Neuralink, aiming to treat chronic health conditions by implanting computer chips directly into the human brain. But that vision may end up taking shape fastest not in the US, but in China, where state authorities have launched a coordinated push to accelerate the country's own brain-computer interface (BCI) industry, according to a South China Morning Post report. China has introduced its first commercial policy covering invasive brain-computer interface (BCI) surgery. State-owned PICC Property and Casualty announced the scheme in partnership with a hospital affiliated with Zhejiang University School of Medicine in Hangzhou, a tech hub home to leading AI and robotics start-ups.Over the past few days, a string of BCI-related initiatives have been announced across China, involving state insurers, investment banks and local governments alike. The most significant came on Wednesday, when PICC Property and Casualty, a major state-owned insurer, announced it had signed the country's first commercial insurance policy covering the invasive surgery typically required to implant a BCI device in a patient's brain.The announcement moved markets almost immediately, with BCI-linked stocks in Hong Kong climbing as investors bet that insurance coverage would help speed up the technology's path to commercial use. Shares of BCI-related firms rose 1.59% on Wednesday, with neuro-interventional device maker Shanghai Heartcare Medical Technology up 1.28% and software developer BrainAurora Medical Technology gaining 1.65%.BCI technology, which conventionally involves open-skull surgery to implant electrodes in a targeted region of the brain, allows patients to control digital devices using thought alone. The field has been most prominently championed globally by Musk's Neuralink, and versions of the technology have already been tested on human patients in both the US and China, in some cases showing promise in helping patients paralysed from the neck down regain the ability to move.The public hospital involved in PICC's new insurance scheme is regarded by local officials and doctors as a leading centre for BCI clinical trials in the region, and has reportedly conducted at least 12 human trials involving BCI implants, according to Chinese media reports. In one recent case, a 61-year-old paraplegic patient with a spinal cord injury regained the ability to bend and lift his leg within three days of surgery, and was walking unassisted by the fifteenth day.Brain-computer interfaces allow signals generated by the brain to be converted into digital commands that can control computers, devices or prosthetics. Musk has repeatedly promoted the technology's potential to transform lives. Speaking via video link at an event in Israel this week, Musk argued that his company, Neuralink, does not receive enough recognition for its achievements."Restoring control of people who are tetraplegics and restoring sight, I think, are pretty big deals," Musk said. "They're sort of what I might call Jesus-level technologies," he added. Neuralink has said its implants could eventually allow users to type, move a computer cursor and operate devices using only their thoughts. Supporters of the technology envision an even more ambitious future, where people could communicate digitally through thoughts or interact with machines without physical input.BCI technology, championed by Elon Musk’s Neuralink, requires open-skull surgery to implant electrodes that allow patients to control digital devices with their thoughts. In Hangzhou, doctors have conducted at least 12 human trials. In one case, a 61-year-old paraplegic regained the ability to walk unassisted within 15 days of surgery.Clinicians cautioned that safety must remain the top priority. “We don’t yet have long-term safety data from BCI clinical trials. There’s no data spanning several years,” said Duan Wanru, chief physician at Xuanwu Hospital in Beijing, during the Global Health Summit in Hong Kong.Alongside the insurance policy, the Zhejiang provincial government announced plans to boost financing for BCI firms and encourage them to go public. The coordinated effort underscores China’s ambition to lead in brain-computer interface technology, potentially outpacing Musk’s vision of “Jesus-level” implants to treat chronic conditions.
Article Summary: China has introduced its first commercial policy covering invasive brain- computer interface (BCI) surgery. BCI technology, championed by Elon Musk’s Neuralink, requires open-skull surgery to implant electrodes that allow patients to control digital devices with their thoughts. In Hangzhou, doctors have conducted at least 12 human trials.

Article Title: America’s biggest investor Michael Burry, who warned Wall Street of 2008 housing crisis, is not happy with Oracle and Micron, here's why
Article Text:
Michael Burry’s concerns about Oracle

The AI hype problem of Micron

Michael Burry is not happy with reports of Nvidia investing $250 billion in OpenAI

America’s biggest investor Michael Burry who famous for warning about the 2008 housing crisis has taken aim at two major technology players Oracle and Micron Technology. According to a report by The Street, known for his contrarian bets, Burry argues that both companies are overexposed to the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom and weighed down by financial commitments that could backfire if demand slows.As per the report, Burry disclosed a short position against Oracle, highlighting its massive spending on AI infrastructure. The company has signed long-term leases and GPU capacity contracts worth hundreds of billions, far exceeding its current revenue base. Despite the strong operating cash flow, Oracle reported negative free cash flow due to surging capital expenditures. Burry warns that if AI demand falters, Oracle could be left with costly obligations and declining returns.Micron Technology is also in Burry’s crosshairs. He expanded his short bet against the chipmaker, arguing its recent rally is driven more by investor enthusiasm for AI than by solid fundamentals. Micron has historically struggled with cyclical downturns, and Burry believes its profitability remains vulnerable despite the current boom.Burry’s bearish stance extends beyond individual companies. He has also shorted the iShares Semiconductor ETF and Nebius Group, signaling broader doubts about the sustainability of AI-linked stocks.His thesis centers on off-balance-sheet liabilities: companies committing billions to long-term infrastructure at inflated prices, which could become burdensome if growth slows.Recently, Michael Burry voiced his sharp criticism of reports that Nvidia is preparing a a $250 billion backstop for OpenAI’s massive Ohio data-center project. According to a report by the Wall Street journal, the guarantees would help OpenAI lease a 10-gigawatt site being developed by SoftBank’s SB Energy, with total costs potentially exceeding $500 billion. Burry’s complaint echoes what analysts have long warned about in AI megadeals: circular funding arrangements that expose investors to enormous risk if sentiment shifts or growth slows. Nvidia, already valued at $5 trillion, has invested $30 billion in OpenAI and is now considering financing chip purchases worth another $350 billion. Critics say such structures could leave the industry vulnerable, especially since OpenAI remains unprofitable and lacks an investment-grade credit rating.Michael Burry’s criticism underscores growing unease about the sustainability of $100 billion-plus AI financing structures. His warning suggests that while AI demand is surging, the industry’s reliance on complex guarantees and debt-backed megaprojects could become its biggest vulnerability.
Article Summary: America's biggest investor Michael Burry has taken aim at two major technology players Oracle and Micron Technology. Burry argues that both companies are overexposed to the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom and weighed down by financial commitments that could backfire if demand slows.

Article Title: Oracle layoffs: As Oracle leadership prepares to send ‘6am layoff email’ on September 1, company asks managers to give a list of…
Article Text:
Oracle cut 21,000 jobs last year. Another round is coming this month

Oracle layoffs in March arrived as 6AM emails for 10,000+ employees and ended the same working day

Oracle has burned through almost all of its $2.1 billion restructuring budget

Why Oracle's $55.7 billion AI data centre spending keeps the pressure on headcount

Oracle is lining up another round of job cuts this month, and the deadline is set by its own calendar. Managers have been asked to draw up lists of employees whose roles are being eliminated, with the company looking to bring payroll down before September 1—the day its fiscal second quarter opens. Business Insider, which first reported the plan citing people familiar with it and an internal document, said reductions on some teams could reach double-digit percentages.The cuts would land on top of a year in which the company already removed about 21,000 full-time roles, roughly 13% of its workforce. Headcount fell from around 162,000 in May 2025 to about 141,000 at the end of May 2026, with roughly 49,000 of those remaining in the United States. What makes this round sting is Oracle's own explanation. Its annual filing attributes part of the decline to the company's adoption and deployment of AI—the same technology it is borrowing tens of billions of dollars to sell.Employees cut on March 31 found out first thing in the morning. The notification, sent from "Oracle Leadership," told recipients their role had been eliminated as part of a broader organisational change and that it was their last working day.Staff in both the US and India were affected. LinkedIn posts from those let go pointed to Oracle Health, Sales, Cloud, Customer Success and NetSuite. Roughly 10,000 positions went in that single wave.The email itself was brisk. It thanked employees for their contributions, told them severance paperwork would arrive via DocuSign, and asked them to submit a personal email address immediately—because access to their computer, email and files was about to be switched off.Severance is not cheap. Oracle booked $1.8 billion in restructuring costs in FY2026, up from $374 million a year earlier, a 391% jump. Its 10-K, filed on June 22, capped the total expected cost of the plan at $2.1 billion, which leaves only about $300 million of headroom. Cuts at the scale Business Insider describes would either have to fit inside that remainder or push Oracle into its second new restructuring plan in three years. TD Cowen analysts estimated in January that shedding 20,000 to 30,000 workers could unlock $8 billion to $10 billion.The money is going somewhere specific. Capital expenditure hit $55.7 billion in FY2026, up from $21.2 billion the year before, as Oracle raced to build data centres for customers including OpenAI. It raised $43 billion in debt and $5 billion in equity over the year, expects around $40 billion more in FY2027, and ran free cash flow of negative $23.7 billion. Interest expense alone climbed to $4.6 billion from $3.6 billion.The underlying business is not the problem. FY2026 revenue rose 17% to $67.4 billion, cloud infrastructure revenue grew 77%, and remaining performance obligations closed the year at $638 billion after ending Q3 at $553 billion. Oracle has also told investors that AI code generation is letting it reorganise product development into smaller teams, saying the technology helps it build "more software in less time with fewer people. "That sentence, written for shareholders in March, reads differently in August. Investors have not been won over either—the stock is down more than 20% this year, and shareholders sued in January over what Oracle said about how much it would need to borrow to service its $300 billion OpenAI commitment.For the employees on this month's lists, the reasoning is beside the point. The jobs are being removed to meet a date on a fiscal calendar, and the payoff Oracle is betting on will arrive after they have gone.
Article Summary: Oracle has burned through almost all of its $2.1 billion restructuring budget. Cuts would land on top of a year in which the company removed about 21,000 full- time roles. The company attributes part of the decline to the company's adoption and deployment of AI.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"

Article Title: How selling Alaska in 1867 was a costly mistake for Russia
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why Russia agreed to the Alaska purchase

The hidden wealth Russia gave away

Strategic and geopolitical consequences







In 1867, Russia’s decision to sell Alaska to America turned out to be a historic mistake that was to go unnoticed for years to come. The sum paid by the US was only $7,200,000. Although, in the light of the circumstances at the time, it appeared logical, retrospectively, the act looks extremely shortsighted. Russia found itself economically constrained, geographically far away from the region and fearful of its falling into the hands of the British without any compensation. In reality, however, the region had proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Its vast reserves of oil, gold, and natural resources would later transform it into one of the most economically significant territories in the United States.The choice of selling Alaska was based on economic and political reasons. By the middle of the 19th century, the Russian Empire experienced financial difficulties as a result of the expensive Crimean War. It had become increasingly hard for the country to manage such remote and thinly populated areas as Alaska.According to EBSCO , “the Russian-American Company was in decline, and the colony failed to yield any profit”.In addition to this, the lucrative fur trade had declined, making the territory much less economically valuable for the empire.At the same time, Russia was afraid that Britain might capture Alaska in case another war broke out between the two countries. Selling the colony to the friendly United States appeared as a logical step. As the Office of the Historian states, William H. Seward, U.S. Secretary of State, “it was a chance to expand its influence in North America and hinder further growth of Britain”.For Russia, the transaction was a chance to minimise the losses. However, it greatly undervalued the potential of Alaska.Another thing that Russia did not expect was the amount of riches that Alaska possessed. Within several decades after the acquisition, the state saw discoveries of enormous deposits of gold, oil, and other minerals.“Alaska has produced more than 40 million ounces of gold,” according to the US Geological Survey. Furthermore, Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) . But even more importantly, the state's oil deposits turned out to be extremely valuable. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968 and became one of North America's biggest.In retrospect, the amount paid by the Americans, $7.2 million, or two cents per acre, was rather laughable. According to Howard I. Kushner , the deal “robbed Russia of an enormously rich territory, the true value of which would only be recognised in the twentieth century.”In addition to resources, there is the question of strategy and how important Alaska is to the United States from a strategic standpoint. This is a very good place when it comes to defence strategy. It borders on the Arctic Ocean and also happens to be close to Russia.During the period of the Cold War, the Alaskan region became a frontier area for the United States, becoming home to military facilities and warning systems.According to Col. Michael J. Forsyth, U.S. Army, the closeness of Russia and Alaska, only about ninety kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, meant that this region became highly significant to the United States' defence plans.From today's point of view, the strategic location of Alaska makes the state very important to the policies of the U.S. related to the Arctic, energy security, and even environmental policies.Thinking back, what seems clear to us now is that the Russians sold Alaska due to immediate needs rather than future considerations. In order to solve the problem, they lost a valuable resource for Russia.Conclusively, the Alaska Purchase should not have been done as it has had a significant impact that will remain throughout history.
Article Summary: Russia sold Alaska to the U.S. in 1867 for only $7,200,000. The sale was based on economic and political reasons. However, the region proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies





AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.
